Now that the complete set of his *Essential Explanations* has been carved for printing, he again requests a preface from me. This brings back to my mind the lectures delivered by the late Master Bai Xue Banglang.
Regarding religion—specifically from within the Great Canon—I have selected eight works to show to others as a ladder for those who study the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna).

He wished to clarify the principles until they were thoroughly understood; thus, his intent was not burdened by brevity. There are *huìshì* (harmonizing expositions) and *shìjì* (explanations of the records), wherein no meaning remains unanalyzed.

Regarding the *Eight Essentials of the Abhidharma School*, since these works were composed in two different lands, they should first be arranged according to their place of origin and then by their chronological order.
Therefore, there is the following proposal for listing the titles and combining them into a single title: [The list follows as indicated.]

I. A Supplementary Discussion on the One Hundred Dharmas: Regarding the *Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra* and the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā*, these were originally composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu to establish the fundamental tenets of the Mahāyāna. It is appropriate to list their titles at the outset.

The original text of this treatise consists solely of the one hundred dharmas and the two forms of selflessness (*anātman*). Master Kuiji later authored a commentary upon it, which remains extant today.
Regarding those who study this, there are occasional points of doubt; therefore, I have again appended these words to explain them, titled *The Supplemental Remarks on the Hundred Dharmas*.
The straight lines below indicate the original treatise by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, while the circles below indicate the commentary composed by Master Ji.
The text: A character missing by one is a redundant addition; it has been set apart as a separate volume.

Second, regarding *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only), there are the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā* (Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only) composed by Vasubandhu, later explained through commentaries by Dharmapāla and others.
These works contain extensive expositions that broadly elaborate upon the refutation of attachments and concisely clarify the underlying principles; these are now frequently cited.
The commentary clarifies the meaning of the principles within the verses; thus, it is titled *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Establishment of Representation-only) according to its intent.
Third, regarding the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Examination of the Object of Cognition), composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga, it is listed next because he followed Vasubandhu.
Subsequently, the Master Dharmapāla composed a commentary to explain its meaning. Now, [the following] is interspersed...
This work cites etymological explanations and correlates them with the treatise, illuminating each other; it is titled *The Commentary on the Synthesis of Terms*.

Fourth, regarding the six types of analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), this section provides a comprehensive explanation of the rules for the six methods of compound formation (*dvandva*, *tatpuruṣa*, etc.). Although the names of the author of the treatise and the translators have been lost, [the work remains].

These were also composed in that land. Because the original texts contained obstructions and difficulties, I have written a few words to facilitate their understanding; thus, the title is "Sixfold Exegesis for Resolving Obstructions.
The three treatises mentioned above were each too short to form a separate volume, so they have been combined into this single work.
V. Commentary on the Explanation of the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*. This was composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla as an exposition of the treatise by the Bodhisattva Dignāga.
It was translated by the Dharma Master Yi Jing of the Tang dynasty. Its phrasing is concise and archaic, and its diction is remarkably unique;
therefore, the text of Dignāga’s treatise is presented in preceding chapters, followed by the commentary of Dharmapāla.
Regarding this: wherever the title of a treatise is followed by "論曰" (lùn yuē), it refers to the text of Dignāga’s treatise.
Wherever it says "釋曰" (shì yuē) or where there is no "釋曰," these are all the explanations by Master Dharmapāla on the treatise. A character set one space lower indicates a recorded word (a gloss).
Therefore, the *Yuanlun shiji* (Record of Explanations on the *Yuanlun*) has been compiled as a separate volume.
Sixth: the *Yinming zhishu* (Direct Commentary on the *Yinming ruzhengli lun*). Its text is concise while its meaning is profound; it is difficult to comprehend at first glance.
I have slightly revised the phrasing and annotated its meaning alongside the text; thus, it is titled the *Zhishu* (Direct Commentary).
VII. The *Sanzhi Yi Chao* (Excerpts on the Meaning of the Three Limbs of Inference): This three-limbed syllogism was established by the Great Master Xuanzang.

Master Yongming Shou had already explained its essential principles within the *Zongjing Lu*, yet there remain certain points where further implications were not fully developed, or where the text was written with brevity.

In summary, I have now briefly excerpted their essential meanings; hence they are given this name. Although the two treatises above were written for two different lands, their textual content and meaning are interrelated;
therefore, I have combined them into a single volume for convenience.
VIII. *Guījù zhèngyì* (The Proof of Meaning through the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses). Composed by Master Xuanzang, this work consists of only twelve verses.
Although Master Tai provided a supplementary commentary based on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there remain omissions in the cited passages of that treatise.
This work now cites those passages to provide proof; hence it is titled *Guījù zhèngyì*. Although Master Xuanzang preceded Master Shou, he is listed first here.

The first point: the meaning is not yet exhaustive.
Regarding what is called "method" (*vidhi*), each section of the text cites a specific rule as a formal model;
by extrapolating and expanding upon these, the principles are fully detailed throughout the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas. Within these, the terminology...
Regarding the term "passing through the barrier" (tōngguān), as there may still be doubts among beginners concerning its significance, I shall provide an explanation to clarify it.
Thus, it is called "passing through the barrier. In the Western [tradition], there are six ways of explaining names (*nirukti*):
first, the dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*); second, the possessive designation (*bahuvrīhi*)... [and so forth].
1. Karma (action), 2. Possessive (sāmi), 3. Contradictory (virodha), 4. Numerical (saṅkhyā), 5. Appositional (upapada), and 6.
Locative (adhikaraṇa). Because these six types involve either separation or combination, each one possesses two aspects.
If a name consists of a single word, it is not a *ṣaṣṭhī-vigraha* (genitive analysis), because separation cannot be established.
Because it is a synthesis of characteristics.
"The Western Regions" refers to the land of the West;
from the Five Indias (Pañcāla) and all other countries, they all explain the meaning of the text by means of this method. As for names and phrases...
Within this, there is the "agent" (neng) and the "object" (suo). Thus, its meaning is clarified by means of the agent and the object;
it is called "the clarification of the agent and the object," following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designation) compound.

If the essence of the meaning itself maintains its functional activity, it is then called "the essence maintaining its functional activity. This is the *karmadhāraya* (maintaining the action) compound.
The *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analysis: if one takes another as a name for the sake of one's own meaning, it is called "designating oneself by means of another.
The *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) analysis: "possessions" (*dhana*) has the sense of the means of livelihood;
because another provides resources for me, it is called "possessing [another]" (*sadhana*). If the meanings are mutually contradictory...
If they do not accord with one another, it is called a "mutual distinction" (*ubhayapada-dvandva*) or a "contradictory analysis" (*vyadhikaraṇa-vigraha*).

If the meaning involves the inclusion of numerical quantity—whether many or few—it is called "substance including quantity" (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*) or a "numeral-inclusive analysis" (*saṃkhyā-vigraha*). If, regarding the characteristics of these respective meanings...
"Adjacent" means residing in close proximity to a powerful neighbor; this is the explanation of "adjacent.

Because these six types each possess both separation and combination, each of the six types is endowed with both aspects, forming the characteristics of separation and combination. If [the term] were a single character alone...

The term "name" (*nāman*) does not follow the format of the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaṭ-samāsa*), because a single word cannot constitute the characteristics of either a *dvandva* (copulative) or a *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) compound.
First, regarding the *tatpuruṣa*: this refers to that which is dependent being the primary element, as in the expression "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Consciousness arises depending on the eye; because it is the consciousness of the eye, it is called "eye-consciousness.
By citing the primary factor (the eye), it indicates the consciousness. This is also termed a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent designation).
This is analogous to taking another's name as a partial designation, such as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) or "consciousness," which is like a son taking his father's name.
Regarding names: when the name depends on its referent, it is called *tatpuruṣa* (dependent designation).
When the father takes the name of the son, it is called *śeṣa* (possessive designation), because that which is depended upon is subordinate. As for the characteristics of separation and combination:
"separation" means that "eye" refers to the sense faculty and "consciousness" refers to discernment; "combination" means that these two combined are designated as "eye."
Consciousness. The combination and separation of the remaining five [aggregates] should be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the fact that the support is primary: "primary" has the sense of being immovable, which serves to reveal the sense of the supported as being adventitious;
for where there is movement, there is coming and going, and existence.
Arising and ceasing. As it is said, the following example is given to clarify the meaning of dependence upon a master.
When consciousness arises in dependence upon the eye, the eye-faculty is permanent, while the consciousness itself arises and ceases.
The consciousness does not name itself; it receives its name by virtue of the eye. This brings forth the [nature of] the eye.
The primary element (the eye) indicates the consciousness; thus it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Therefore, it is termed *tatpuruṣa* (dependent on the primary).
It is also termed *śeṣa* (dependent on the secondary): that same aforementioned eye-consciousness is also called *śeṣa*.
The former name (*cakṣurvijñāna*) was explained as *tatpuruṣa*; this [latter] name is... [the explanation of the term *śeṣa*].

Regarding the term "dependent" (*tatpuruṣa*): this explains the meaning of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Because consciousness is named after the eye, it is called "the consciousness belonging to the eye";
thus, it is termed "dependent. When the eye is named after consciousness, it is called "eye-consciousness";
because it takes form as its object, it is termed "dependent," where "dependent" (*tad*) refers to that which is based upon [the object]. "Dependent" (*tad*) is precisely...
The meaning of "son" (*putra*) is as follows: the sense faculty (*indriya*) is capable of producing consciousness; thus, the faculty receives the name of "father," while consciousness is the "son.
Since consciousness is able to discern form (*rūpa*), it is called "eye-consciousness perceiving form."
This is an *upapada* (dependent) compound. Regarding "appropriating the name of another": when consciousness takes up the name "eye," it is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound;
when the eye takes up the name "consciousness," it is an *upapada* compound. Both are termed "appropriating.
As for the phrase "name-and-form-consciousness," this refers to consciousness based upon its object, name-and-form, and is thus a metaphor.

The primary basis is the sense organ; the name "eye-consciousness" (cakṣurvijñāna) is formed by the two compounds *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive), just as in the example of a "son.

Because the basis is inferior—meaning that consciousness is superior while the sense organ is inferior—the sense organ receives the designation of "consciousness," and thus it is called "eye-consciousness" because it can cognize.
A separate color. This means that the consciousness which is the supported (āśrita) is superior, while the sense faculty which is the support (āśraya) is inferior.
Regarding the phrase "separation and conjunction below," this explains that all six types possess both separation and conjunction;
therefore, it says, "the separation and conjunction of the remaining five should be understood by analogy with this."

Regarding the term "retainer-of-activity" (*dharmadhara*): as it is said concerning the *ālayavijñāna*, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the essence (*svabhāva*), while "store" (*ālaya*) refers to the activity (*karman*).
Activity can manifest the essence, and the essence can sustain the activity.
Since the store is itself consciousness, it is called the "store-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*); thus, it is termed a "retainer-of-activity. It is also called "identical" (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
According to the commentary: "Ālaya" (the storehouse) takes the function of containing and storing; "vijñāna" (consciousness) takes the function of cognizing and discerning.
Since these two share the same basis, they are said to be "co-dependent.
The *ālayavijñāna* is the eighth consciousness; because it possesses the function of containing and storing, it is so named.
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*: if "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the essence (*tattva*), it is called "store" (*ālaya*) because consciousness is capable of initiating karma.
If karma is the function (*karman*), then since karma arises from consciousness, the essence is manifested through karma;
and since the essence sustains the function, the function is itself the essence—this is termed "sustaining the function" (*dharmadharmatā*).
Explanation: It is also called "having a common basis" because the two meanings of the *ālayavijñāna* share a single substratum.
The *ālaya* (storehouse) is that which stores; its function is containment.
The *vijñāna* (consciousness) is the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*); its function is discernment. [Thus,] it contains and it discerns.
All [these] rely upon the substance of consciousness, sharing the same substance as the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvedana-bhāga); therefore, they are called "sharing the same basis" (*samāśraya*).
As for the term "possessive" (*sadhana*), it means that the name is derived from that which is possessed. First.
"Buddha" is here translated as "the Awakened One" (覺者). That is, one who possesses awakening is called an "Awakened One.
This is an instance of adopting the name of another [term]. Second, as in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
It is not the Abhidharmakośa itself; "Abhidharmakośa" is the name of the root treatise.
Because this work was composed based upon that root Abhidharmakośa, it is also called the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
This is a case of adopting the name of another in its entirety, and it is also termed a *matup-puruṣa* (possessive) compound.
"Wealth" (*dhana*) carries the meaning of "providing benefit. Because it provides resources for oneself, it is called "possessing wealth" (*sadhana*).
Since another [thing] is what one possesses, it is said that the name is derived from that which is possessed.
For example, *buddha* is translated here as "the Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*).
The following provides an example to explain the term "possessing wealth" (*sādhana*). The character "awakening" (*jue*) signifies "other," while the character "that" (*zhe*) signifies "self.
The combination of self and other is termed "appropriation" (*vibhāga*).
This *Abhidharmakośa*—here translated as the *Treasury of Abhidharma* (*Abhidharmapiṭaka*)—was composed based upon this *Abhidharmapiṭaka*.
The treatise is also called the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. This is an adoption of another name in its entirety;
it is also an example of a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).
Regarding the term "contradictory," it refers to what is said concerning the eye, the ear, and so forth, each being distinct.
Explanation: These all function as primary subjects and do not accord with one another; therefore, they are said to be "contradictory" (*viruddha*).

This applies to the two terms "ear" and "eye," and does not conform to the previous two interpretations. The meaning here extends to both the *saṃkhyeya* (possessing a number) and the *matup* (possessive) types of compounds.
"Regarding the eye, ear, and so forth": "and so forth" refers to the nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye designates and takes form as its object;
likewise, up to the mind, which designates and takes phenomena (dharma) as its object.
Therefore, it is said that they each have their own distinct objects designated and each serves as a basis for the arising of its respective consciousness. They are mutually [distinct].
They do not borrow from one another; therefore, it is said that each acts as its own master.
Since they act as their own masters, there is no sense of conformity; thus, they are said to be "in opposition. This refers to the passage beginning with "for the ear," etc.
This interpretation of the contradiction is distinct from other interpretations in that it does not allow for mutual interchangeability.
Regarding the terms "ear" (*karṇa*) and "eye" (*cakṣus*), both the Southern and Northern editions erroneously read them as "existence" (*asti*) and "with" (*ca*);
they have now been corrected according to the meaning. These refer to the aforementioned two: the eye and the ear.
The statement "these two terms" refers to the *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) analysis.
This differs from the previous explanation regarding the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analyses, which apply to the remaining two types of analysis as well.
The *tatpuruṣa* analysis includes those with a numeral (*saṃkhyā-bahuvrīhi*), while the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) and *karmadhāraya* analyses also include those with a numeral (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*).
Therefore, regarding what is called "indicating by number," it clarifies the meaning through numerical designation and applies to all three types of explanation,
as in the cases of the "five aggregates" and the "two truths. Here, "five" is itself the aggregates, and "two" is itself the truths.
This usage, where the term is applied to itself, constitutes a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) with an included number (*saṃkhyānvita*).
For example, the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take themselves and others as their names; this constitutes an *upapada* (dependent compound) with an included number.
As it is said that the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) are the "five [acts] without interval" (*pañcānantaryāṇi*): "without interval" (*ānantarya*) is the result, which is [here] the cause.
Regarding the discussion of results (*phala*): this [term] entirely adopts the name of another, which constitutes "possessing an attribute" (*saviśeṣaṇa*) and "involving a number" (*saṃkhyānvita*).
That is to say, when a name or phrase is accompanied by a number or quantity, it is called "involving a number.

Alternatively, it may employ only its own [name], in which case it is a "function-as-substance" (*karmadhāraya*); or it may employ only that of another, in which case it is a "possessive compound" (*tatpuruṣa*).

There is the "possessor of wealth" (tatpuruṣa) compound, which may involve both self and other; because it applies universally as a dependent-determinative (tatpuruṣa), it is said to apply to the other three types of compounds as well.

Regarding the "five aggregates," "two truths," and so forth—the term "and so forth" includes the remaining [categories] such as the three bodies, the four wisdoms, up to the nine meditative absorptions and the ten dhyānas—all of these are termed "possessors" (dhāraka).
Regarding number: the aggregates (skandha) have the number five; the five themselves are the aggregates. The truths (satya) have the number two;
the two themselves are the truths. Since these all take their own [constituent] as their name, each is termed "possessing its own function" (dharmadhāra).
In the case of the five and the two, it is termed "bearing [the number]" (paryāpanna).
Number. Furthermore, among the six consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness, consciousness itself is the "self" (sva) and the eye and so forth are the "other" (para).
Because it is a compound name formed by combining "self" and "other," it is called *tatpuruṣa* (dependent on another).
Because there are six types, it is further called *saṃkhyā-viśiṣṭa* (possessing number). It is like when someone scolds:
To revile one who has committed the five heinous crimes (ānantarya) is termed the "five types of immediate retribution" (*pañcānantaryajāti*).
By adopting the name of the result in its entirety to represent the five heinous crimes, this refers exclusively to the other [the cause] and is thus called "possessing wealth" (*sadhana*).
Since both cause and effect each consist of five kinds, it is further termed "indicating number" (*saṃkhyāvadhi*).
Regarding the term "proximate" (*sāmantaka*): it is named according to its proximity.
For example, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have wisdom as their essence; because wisdom is proximate to mindfulness, they are called "foundations of mindfulness.

Since this is a case of proximity, it is not like [a term] functioning as its own referent (*svabhāva-karmadhāraya*); thus, it does not carry the sense of being self-sustaining, but rather applies to the other two types of compounds.
Explanation: First is the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) based on proximity. For example, suppose there is a person living near Chang’an.
Someone asks, "Where do you live? and he replies, "I live in Chang’an."
This person is not from Chang’an; however, because they are near Chang’an, they are said to “dwell in Chang’an.
This is an example of *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) based on proximity, as well as *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound) based on proximity.
For instance, when asked, "Where is this person from? one replies, "Chang’an."
Taking the entirety of another location to designate a person's name constitutes the "possessor" (sadvat).
Because it is near Chang'an, it is further called "Neighboring" (Linjin).
Being adjacent and proximate, it borrows that [name] as its designation; therefore, it is named "Neighboring."

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: they consist of distinct recollections—contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self—all of which are observed with the wisdom of decisive discernment.
As for why these are called "mindfulness," it is because they arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Mindfulness arises; wisdom is born from concentration. Because mindfulness and wisdom are adjacent to one another, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
This is based on the meaning of proximity. Whenever something is said to be proximate, there must necessarily be both self and other;
therefore, this differs from the previous case where the name was derived from its own function. There is no [separate] maintenance.
Explanation of the compound: It is explained solely through the two types of analysis, *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive).
First, regarding the *tatpuruṣa*, it is further analyzed as a *sāmānādhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa* (co-referential dependent). As for the phrase "dwelling in Chang'an":
"Chang'an" is the external referent (*para*), while "dweller" is the internal referent (*ātman*). The name [“dweller in Chang’an”] is formed by combining both the internal and external referents.
Therefore, it is said that they are "partially taken. Regarding the second [type], "possessing property" (*sāmiṣa*), the subsequent explanation clarifies its proximity to "possessing property.
As for the term "Cháng'ān," it employs only the name of another; therefore, it is called "fully taken.
The verse says:
"Functioning for oneself and functioning for others; neither for oneself nor for others;

both—these six types of explanation clarify the general verse’s sixfold analysis of names and meanings through the methods of *nirukti* (etymological analysis) and *samāsa* (compound analysis). Now, furthermore:
I shall now compose verses to explain the meaning of these stanzas:
The *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) employs only its own [meaning]; The *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) employs only that which belongs to another;
The *bahuvrīhi* (exocentric compound) employs both its own and that of another; The *dvandva* (copulative compound) employs neither.
The term "proximate" (*upapada*) admits of two interpretations:
namely, as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound), a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound), and one involving a numeral or an intensifying particle (*karmadhāraya*).
Thus, these six types of interpretation—may they be understood by all.
